## plugin:deepwork:deepwork
## Available Workflows

This project uses DeepWork. If the user wants to do something matching these, use `/deepwork` to start the workflow.

- **deepplan** (create_deep_plan): Structured planning workflow that produces an executable DeepWork job definition
- **deepwork_jobs** (new_job, repair, learn, shared_jobs): Creates and manages multi-step AI workflows. Use when defining, implementing, testing, or improving DeepWork jobs.
- **deepwork_reviews** (discover_rules, add_document_update_rule): Manage .deepreview rules for automated code review

# DeepWork Workflow Server

Multi-step workflows with quality gates.

**Session identity**: On Claude Code pass `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` as `session_id`. On other platforms omit `session_id` in `start_workflow`; the server auto-generates one and returns it in `begin_step.session_id` — use that value for all subsequent calls. Sub-agents on Claude Code also pass `agent_id` (CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_ID).

## Workflow Lifecycle

1. `get_workflows` — discover available workflows
2. `start_workflow` — begin with goal, job_name, workflow_name (session_id optional — see above)
3. Follow step instructions; use `begin_step.session_id` for all subsequent calls, then call `finished_step` with outputs
4. If `needs_work`: fix issues and retry. If `next_step`: continue. If `workflow_complete`: done.

Workflows nest via stack. Use `abort_workflow` to cancel, `go_to_step` to revisit earlier steps.

Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

5d5c4cd test: assert values, not structural guarantees, in thirteen places (#449)
05bb512 test: make the fixture reach the branch in seven tests (#447)

9625e84 test: assert the answer, not the agreement, in six tests (#445)

---440---
test: seven tests whose fixture makes the branch they name unreachable
From the suite-wide tautology audit. In each of these the fixture guarantees the assertion, so the code path the test is *named for* never executes. Deleting that code path leaves the test green.

Confidence from reading plus in-memory mutant runs by the auditing pass; `bench/mutate.py` can confirm any of them mechanically.

## The tests

**1. `tests/test_layers.py:722` `test_glob_patterns_never_hint`**
The pattern `shipping.store.**` matches both fixture nodes, so `unlayered_modules == ()`. `_exact_pattern_hints` iterates only over `unlayered`, so it returns `()` for any pattern shape. The `if "*" in pattern: continue` skip, the entire subject, is never reached. Deleting that line keeps the test green.
*Fix:* add an unlayered descendant, e.g. a third node under a `shipping.store.*` pattern.

**2. `tests/test_layers.py:232` `test_violations_ignores_unlayered_endpoints`**
Config is built with `forbid=()`, so `find_violations` returns `[]` at `forbid_index.get(...) -> None` for any graph and any layer-matching behaviour. The `src_layer is None or tgt_layer is None` guard it is named for is not exercised, and no `Violation` can be constructed without a rule, so no mutation turns it red. The guard is currently untested.
*Fix:* use the `core_cli_config` fixture (which has a real rule) with an unlayered source.

**3. `tests/test_graph.py:68` `test_package_init_edges_skip_external_nodes`**
`package_init_edges` loops `for i in range(1, len(parts))` over dotted segments, and `_external_target` collapses every external import to a **single-segment** name, so `"requests"` can never appear on either side with or without the guard. Deleting both external guards leaves the edge list unchanged.

**4. `tests/test_graph.py:422` `test_graph_to_dict_is_deterministic`** (node half only)
Discovery already yields `['pkg','pkg.a','pkg.b','pkg.c']`, so `node_ids == sorted(node_ids)` holds without the `sorted()` in `graph_to_dict`. The edge half IS load-bearing (raw order is deliberately reversed), so only half this test is dead.

**5. `tests/test_score.py:67` `test_modularity_clamps_to_zero_on_negative_q`**
On the 4-node complete digraph `greedy_modularity_communities` returns one community and `raw_q == 0.0`, so Q is never negative and `max(0.0, ...)` never fires. Deleting the clamp entirely keeps the score at 0.3333 and the test green. No negative-Q graph is constructed anywhere in the file.

**6. `tests/test_mcp.py:764` `test_snapshot_brief_load_bearing_ranked_and_capped`**
`compute_edit_risk` returns `0.0` for all three fixture modules, and a list of identical values is sorted in **both** directions, so inverting the ranking key passes. The cap is 5 and the fixture can only produce 3, so `len(...) <= 5` holds with the cap removed (`_BRIEF_LOAD_BEARING_N = 1_000_000` verified green).
*Fix:* a fixture with distinct non-zero risks and more than 5 modules.

**7. `tests/test_duplicates.py:704` `test_near_miss_clusters_gapped_clone`** (similarity assertion)
`assert g.similarity >= 0.8` is called with `min_similarity=0.8`, and `compute_near_duplicates` only records an edge when `sim >= min_similarity`. Every group it can return satisfies this. Replacing Jaccard with containment inflates similarities and the assertion still reads `>= 0.8`.

## Common shape

Each of these would be fixed by making the fixture reach the branch: a value outside the clamp, a rule that can fire, a node the pattern does not match, risks that differ. The audit's own lesson from #437 applies: **assert the fixture exercises the thing before asserting the outcome**, so the test cannot quietly stop testing.

## Related

- #438 the two gaps where a bug ships silently
- #439 tests that compare a function against itself
STATE: closed

content.content:
bench: the arm-interleaving invariant is asserted against a list the test builds itself

From the suite-wide tautology audit. Filed separately from #439/#440/#441 because this one is in a **measurement harness**, where AGENTS.md's rule applies directly: a harness bug found during a paid agent run is a run wasted, and these two tests are named for the property that makes chunked batches interpretable at all.

## The two tests

`tests/test_greenfield_run.py:633` `test_every_chunk_contains_both_arms` and
`tests/test_greenfield_run.py:721` `test_arms_are_interleaved_so_a_partial_batch_stays_balanced`

Both **rebuild the unit list inside the test** and assert on their own comprehension:

```python
units = [(f"conduit-{i:02d}", arm) for i in range(1, 4) for arm in ("A", "B")]
assert units[:2] == [("conduit-01", "A"), ("conduit-01", "B")]
```

`bench/greenfield_run.py:753`'s own `units` is never consulted. The second test is the more misleading of the two: it monkeypatches `run_with_limit_backoff` to append into `seen` and calls `main()`, but passes `--dry-run`, which returns at line 755 **before the loop**, so the stub never fires and `seen` is never asserted on. The only way either test fails is if `main()` raises.

## Verified

Applying the exact defect they are named for, arm-major ordering:

```python
units = [(unit_id(i), arm) for arm in arms for i in range(1, args.limit + 1)]
```

def test_raising_the_limit_only_adds_work(batch, monkeypatch, tmp_path):
    """Chunking works because unit ids are stable: a later, larger --limit runs
    the new units and leaves the earlier ones alone."""
    seen: list[str] = []

        "conduit-03:B",
        "conduit-04:A",
        "conduit-04:B",
    ]

Do not proceed with reviews until the agent is available.

## How to Run

1. Call the `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` tool directly:
   - **No arguments** to review the current branch's changes (auto-detects via git diff against the main branch).
   - **With `files`** to review only specific files: `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions(files=["src/app.py", "src/lib.py"])`. When provided, only reviews whose include/exclude patterns match the given files will be returned. Use this when the user asks to review a particular file or set of files rather than the whole branch.

3. **While review agents run**, check for a changelog and open PR (see below).
4. Collect the results from all review agents.

## Changelog & PR Description Check

Run this concurrently with the review agents (step 2 above) — don't wait for reviews to finish first.

name: archy-next-up
description: "Where archy stands as of 2026-09-05 and what to pick up next: #442 is the last of the tautology audit and its ticket carries a start-here comment. Holds the release/pypi-gate/gh-REST conventions."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

  modified: 2026-09-04T17:58:26.082Z
---

**NEXT SESSION STARTS WITH #442**, the last of the tautology audit. **Read the
"Start here next session" comment on the ticket first** (posted 2026-09-05): it
names the two tests, the concrete fix, the arm-major mutation to verify with,
and the traps. #440 closed via #447 (seven tests, ten mutants) and #441 via
#449 (thirteen sites, thirteen mutants); every fix in both was verified by
mutation, which is the only method that has worked on this class.

## Where things stand, 2026-09-05

archy is ACTIVE (see [[archy-wound-down]], which is superseded) and **v0.46.0 is
on PyPI**. `main` is green at 1,224 tests, at `5d5c4cd`.

Shipped in the 2026-09-04/05 session: #440 (#447) and #441 (#449), which
between them closed all but one of the tautology audit. Four tickets were split
out of review rounds rather than folded into either PR: #448, #450, #451, #452.

Shipped in the 2026-09-02 session: v0.46.0 release, the reopen (#425), #343
closed via #426, #429's precision pilot returning null (#430), `--emit-headers`
(#432) dogfooded and CI-gated (#434), shared import resolution (#437), the
mutation harness (#443), and two tautology tickets closed (#444, #445).

## The tautology audit, which is the live thread

A suite-wide audit found ~16 tests that assert something true regardless of
whether the code is correct. Filed as #438-#442; **#438, #439 and #440 are
closed**, and so is **#441** (merged as #447 and #449); **only #442
remains**.

**The rule, now in `AGENTS.md` under "Tests that cannot fail":** a green suite is
not evidence a test works. Change the code a test covers and check it goes red.
`bench/mutate.py` does it in bulk.

**Do not trust a reading pass on this.** Five consecutive review rounds each
found a test the previous round had declared sound, three of them in tests
written specifically to close this class of gap. A static audit also produced
two confident claims that were false when run.

## Open, roughly by value

- **#442** the bench arm-interleaving tests, which assert on a list they build
  themselves (NEXT, and the last of the audit)
- **#450** `is_relative` is first-seen-wins, so a mixed import pair
  under-reports; found while fixing #441, needs a DECISION (three options in
  the ticket) before a patch, because option 1 is wire-visible on all three
  surfaces
- **#435** a real `contracts` bug the user set aside on 2026-09-02
- **#436** which re-export target is right (a decision, not a refactor)
- **#428** headers exist but are UNMEASURED; the local-rig arm is what settles it
- refactor backlog: #415, #416, #419 (done), #413, #411, #388, #422
- test-hygiene backlog, all split out of review rounds this session: #448
  (hoist a local import), #451 and #452 (duplicated test scaffolding, same
  shape as #186, #370, #411, #413)
- docs: #405, #417, #433

## Conventions this session confirmed

- Release: bump `pyproject.toml`, `src/archy/__init__.py`, `server.json` (x2),
  `uv.lock`, README status + both CI pins; tag via a GitHub release, then
  approve the `pypi` env gate ([[approve-pypi-gate-via-api]]).
- Always `gh api` REST ([[github-rest-not-graphql]]).
- Review via DeepWork ([[use-deepwork-review]]); it earns its keep, finding real
  bugs in nearly every round on this repo.
- CI gates now include `archy conventions . --emit-headers --check`; regenerate
  with `--write`, never hand-edit a block.

graph: `is_relative` is first-seen-wins, so a mixed import pair under-reports

Found while fixing #441 (PR #449) and split out, because it is behaviour, not a test.

## What happens

`_add_or_extend_edge` (`src/archy/graph.py:647`) sets `is_relative` only on the branch that CREATES the edge:

```python
if graph.has_edge(src, dst):
    data["lines"] = (*data.get("lines", ()), ref.line)
    ...                      # is_relative is not touched
else:
    graph.add_edge(src, dst, is_relative=ref.is_relative, ...)
```

So for a module that imports the same target twice, the FIRST import decides the flag for the pair:

```python
# pkg/a.py
from pkg.b import x   # line 2, absolute  -> creates the edge, is_relative=False
from .b import y      # line 3, relative  -> extends lines, flag untouched
```

`pkg.a -> pkg.b` reports `lines=(2, 3)` and `is_relative=False`, though one of the two contributing imports is relative. Written the other way round, the same pair reports `True`.

Verified on the current tree; `tests/test_mcp.py::test_graph_focus_preserves_edge_attributes` now pins both directions, so the behaviour is covered either way and this ticket is about whether it is the RIGHT behaviour.

## Why it might matter

`archy_graph_focus` documents `is_relative` as what distinguishes `from .x import y` from an absolute import, and an agent reading `is_relative=False` will reasonably conclude there is no relative import on that edge. On a mixed pair that conclusion is wrong, and the flag is first-seen rather than anything an agent could predict. The test that covered this carried a comment claiming last-seen-wins, which suggests the current semantics were not deliberate.

## Options

1. **`any`**: OR the flag on extend, so `is_relative` means "at least one contributing import was relative". Matches how `lines` already aggregates, and matches the reading an agent is most likely to take.
2. **Per-line**: carry the flag alongside each entry in `lines`, so a caller can see which import site was relative. More faithful, wider payload change across the CLI JSON and the MCP models.
3. **Document it**: keep first-seen and say so in the field description and the tool docs.

Option 1 looks right, but it is a wire-visible change on three surfaces (`_graph_focus_to_text`/`_to_dict` in `src/archy/cli.py` and the tool return model in `src/archy/mcp.py`), so it wants a decision before a patch.

## Related

- #441, where the vacuous assertion that hid this (`edge.is_relative in (True, False)`) was replaced.

from .b import y      # line 3, relative  -> extends lines, flag untouched
```

`archy_graph_focus` documents `is_relative` as what distinguishes `from .x import y` from an absolute import, and an agent reading `is_relative=False` will reasonably conclude there is no relative import on that edge. The test that covered this carried a comment claiming last-seen-wins, which suggests the current semantics were not deliberate.

2. **Per-line**: carry the flag alongside each entry in `lines`, so a caller can see which import site was relative. More faithful, wider payload change across the CLI JSON and the MCP models.
3. **Document it**: keep first-seen and say so in the field description and the tool docs.

Closes #450. Option 1 from the ticket.

## The bug

`_add_or_extend_edge` set `is_relative` only on the branch that *creates* the edge, so when a module imported the same target twice the first import decided the flag for the whole pair:

```python
# pkg/a.py
from pkg.b import x   # line 2, absolute -> creates the edge, is_relative=False
from .b import y      # line 3, relative -> extends lines, flag untouched
```

`pkg.a -> pkg.b` reported `lines=(2, 3)` and `is_relative=False`, though one of the two contributing imports is relative. Written the other way round, the same pair reported `True`.

`archy_graph_focus` documents `is_relative` as what distinguishes `from .x import y` from an absolute import, so an agent reading `False` reasonably concludes there is no relative import on that edge. On a mixed pair that is wrong, and the value was first-seen rather than anything a caller could predict.

A prior adversarial review round had already recorded this exact defect (`docs/research/adversarial_2026_06/round1_findings.md:994`); it was confirmed then and never fixed.

## The fix

OR on extend, so `is_relative` means "at least one contributing import was relative". This aggregates the way `lines` already does, and it is order-independent.

## Surfaces

Three surfaces read this flag: the `build_graph` docstring where it is specified, the CLI JSON via `graph_to_dict`, and the MCP `GraphEdge` return model. Only one code site changes, because every surface reads the attribute the graph builder sets, so this is the fix-at-the-source case rather than the three-surfaces gap AGENTS.md warns about. The tests cover each surface anyway, since that is where a regression would actually be observed.

## Functional tests

Six, every one building real files on disk and going through `build_graph` or the command under test. None asserts against a graph the test hand-assembles, and each asserts the fixture reaches the extend branch (`lines` has more than one entry) before asserting the flag, so a test cannot quietly stop testing if its fixture drifts.

Scenarios: `from X import name` in both orders; the `import pkg.b` / `from . import b` forms, which take a different route through the parser; a three-site pair with the relative import in the middle; and an all-absolute pair that must stay `False`.

| mutation | tests that go red |
|---|---|
| remove the OR (back to first-seen) | 6: the mixed pair, both import-form variants, the three-site case, both MCP tests, the CLI JSON test |

Here's where the tests stand after your prompt to scrutinize them.

**The tests are functional, not tautological.** All six build real `.py` files on disk and go through `build_graph` or the actual command under test. None asserts against a graph the test hand-assembles, and each asserts the fixture reaches the extend branch (`lines` has more than one entry) *before* asserting the flag, so a test can't quietly stop testing if its fixture drifts.

Mutation-verified, `__pycache__` cleared between runs. Every test is killed by at least one mutant:

| mutation | tests that go red |
|---|---|
| drop the OR (back to first-seen) | 6: mixed pair, both import-form variants, three-site case, both MCP tests, CLI JSON test |
| `= True` | the all-absolute test |
| `= ref.is_relative` (last-seen) | the reversed-order test and the three-site case |

**Scenarios I added after your message**, because the original three were thin on real-world import forms:
- `import pkg.b` + `from . import b` — a different route through the parser than `from X import name`, and the pair a real package actually writes
- a three-site pair with the relative import in the middle, which pins that `any` holds across *every* later extend, not just the one following the relative import

**I also caught a false claim of my own.** The first commit message said the fix "also fixes the call-only edge path" at `graph.py:686`. That's wrong: `assemble_graph` adds every import edge in a complete first pass (`graph.py:231`) before any call edge (`graph.py:252`), so `_add_or_extend_edge` can never see an edge seeded by `_add_or_extend_call_edge`. The path is unreachable. I amended the commit to remove it rather than leave an untested assertion in the history, and the PR body now says so explicitly.

**Review round on #454:** 6 of 8 passed. The two that failed found only pre-existing issues in files this PR touches, so per AGENTS.md they were filed, not folded in: **#455** (`_git` re-imports `subprocess` locally, and one test hand-rolls the call it wraps, both in `test_mcp.py`), and the `test_graph.py` inline-fixture duplication, which was already open as **#186**.

One more thing worth flagging: a reviewer found this exact bug was already recorded as a confirmed finding in `docs/research/adversarial_2026_06/round1_findings.md:994`. It was spotted in an adversarial round months ago and never fixed.

Gates all green: 1,231 tests passing (up 7), plus ruff, ty, and archy's three self-checks. A final review round on `test_graph.py` is running.

fix(contracts): archy contracts reports a clean pass on a forbidden transitive path

`archy contracts` reports a clean pass on a project that has a forbidden transitive path. The contract is listed as `OK`, the exit code is 0, and nothing indicates that anything was skipped.

Reproduced on `main` at `cac8bed`.

## Reproduction

```
shipping/__init__.py        (empty)
shipping/api.py             VALUE = 1
shipping/service.py         from shipping import api
shipping/store.py           from shipping import service
```

`archy.yaml`:

```yaml
layers:
  api:
    modules: ["shipping.api.**"]
  service:
    modules: ["shipping.service.**"]
  store:
    modules: ["shipping.store.**"]

forbid:
  - {from: store, to: api}
```

`store` reaches `api` through `service`. That is exactly what a `forbid` rule plus a transitive checker exists to catch.

```
$ uv run --extra contracts archy contracts .
# contracts: 1 kept, 0 broken (4 modules, 2 imports)
OK store layer must not reach api layer  [ForbiddenContract]
```

The module and import counts are right — 4 modules, 2 imports — so the graph is complete. The verdict is not.

## Why this is worse than a missed violation

**`contracts` is the surface users are told to reach for when `check` is not enough.** `contracts.py`'s own docstring describes it as *"a strictness upgrade over `archy check` (direct edges only)"*, and `check` says the same thing in its output when coverage is thin:

```
$ uv run archy check .
# No layer violations (config: ./archy.yaml).
#   layer coverage: 3 of 4 modules (75%), 2 of 2 internal edges (100%); 1 module(s) match no layer
#   1 forbid rule declared, but this check governs too little of the graph to verify them.
```

So the tool correctly says "`check` cannot verify this, go and use the transitive path" — and the transitive path then returns a clean pass. A user following the documented advice ends up more confident and no better protected.

**`check` is not at fault here.** 100% edge coverage is true: both direct edges run between layered modules. Coverage measures governance, not detection. Only the transitive checker could have caught this, and it reported success.

## Relationship to #387

This is the vacuity failure #387 already anticipates, arriving from a different direction. That issue puts it as:

> a reach assertion over an under-connected graph passes vacuously

and argues that any required-reach implementation needs a negative control in its own suite — a fixture with the reaching edge removed, which the check must fail on. The same argument applies to the existing `forbidden` path, and the case above is a live instance of it rather than a hypothetical.

Whatever the resolution, the general shape seems worth fixing directly: **a contract that could not have failed should not be reported the same way as a contract that was evaluated and held.** `OK` and "not actually checked" are different facts and the output currently conflates them.

## Scope

- Affects `archy contracts` and the `archy_contracts` MCP tool.
- Not layer-config-specific: any project whose layers are written in the form above.
- Exit code is 0, so CI passes.

## Note on this report

I have a verified root-cause analysis and a tested patch for this, and I am deliberately not including either here. They are being held back for a short period for an unrelated evaluation that uses this repository at a pinned commit, and publishing the diagnosis would invalidate it.

That is a poor reason from the project's point of view, so: **say the word and I will post the analysis and open a PR immediately.** The patch passes the full suite (1110 passed, 2 skipped), `ruff`, and `bench/walkthrough.py`, and it also adds a flag so a contract that matches nothing can no longer read as a clean pass.

Filing the symptom now rather than sitting on the whole thing, since the impact is silent and users are affected today.

## Status caveat

archy is in maintenance (#383). Filing as a record of a verified defect rather than as scheduled work.

content.text:
Root cause found, and it's sharper than the ticket states:

- archy's `X.**` means "X **and** all descendants" (`layers.py:914`)
- import-linter's `X.**` means "descendants of X only", excluding X

So `shipping.store.**` resolves to the **empty set**, the contract has no source modules, and import-linter vacuously keeps it. Since AGENTS.md tells users to write `pkg.**` rather than `pkg`, the recommended form is exactly the one that silently disables every derived contract.

import sys
import warnings
from pathlib import Path
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

from archy.layers import LayerConfig, LayerConfigError, load_config

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from importlinter.application.user_options import UserOptions


class ContractCheck(BaseModel):
    """One contract's result. `metadata` is the import-linter contract-type-
    specific shape (e.g., `invalid_chains` for ForbiddenContract); kept opaque
    here so the wrap doesn't need to know every contract type's schema."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    name: str
    contract_type: str
    kept: bool
    metadata: dict[str, object]
    warnings: tuple[str, ...]


class ContractsResult(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    kept: int
    broken: int
    module_count: int
    import_count: int
    contracts: tuple[ContractCheck, ...] = ()

    @property
    def all_kept(self) -> bool:
        return self.broken == 0


class ContractsNotAvailable(RuntimeError):
    """Raised when `import-linter` is not installed."""


class ContractsConfigError(RuntimeError):
    """Raised when the .importlinter file is missing or invalid."""


def run_contracts(
    project_dir: Path,
    config_filename: str | Path | None = None,
) -> ContractsResult:
    """Run import-linter against `project_dir` and return a structured result.

    `project_dir` must contain (or be the parent of) an importable copy of
    the package(s) named in the config; import-linter's graph builder uses
    runtime `import` resolution.

    Config resolution: `config_filename` (if given) wins; otherwise prefers
    `.importlinter` in `project_dir`; otherwise falls back to translating
    `archy.yaml` into Forbidden contracts. Raises `ContractsConfigError`
    if none are present.
    """
    try:
        from importlinter import configuration as _configuration  # noqa: F401
    except ImportError as exc:
        raise ContractsNotAvailable(
            "import-linter is not installed. "
            "Install with `pip install archy[contracts]` to use this feature."
        ) from exc
=== drive
def _drive_import_linter(
    *,
    config_path: Path | None = None,
    user_options: UserOptions | None = None,
) -> ContractsResult:
    """The narrow surface we depend on inside import-linter.

    Either pass `config_path` (we delegate reading to import-linter's
    INI/TOML readers) or pass pre-built `user_options` (used when we
    derive contracts from archy.yaml). Imports are deferred so the
    optional-dep guard in `run_contracts` triggers first.
    """
    from importlinter import configuration
    from importlinter.application.use_cases import (
        _register_contract_types,
        create_report,
        read_user_options,
    )

    configuration.configure()
    prior_cwd = Path.cwd()
    try:
        if user_options is None:
            assert config_path is not None
            # import-linter's INI reader resolves config_filename relative to
            # cwd; chdir into the config's directory for the duration of
            # read+report, then restore.
            os.chdir(config_path.parent)
            user_options = read_user_options(config_filename=config_path.name)
        _register_contract_types(user_options)
        report = create_report(user_options, cache_dir=None)
    finally:
        os.chdir(prior_cwd)

    contracts: list[ContractCheck] = []
    for contract, check in report.get_contracts_and_checks():
        contracts.append(
            ContractCheck(
                name=str(contract.name),
                contract_type=type(contract).__name__,

from pathlib import Path
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

from archy.layers import LayerConfig, LayerConfigError, load_config

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from importlinter.application.user_options import UserOptions


class ContractCheck(BaseModel):
    """One contract's result. `metadata` is the import-linter contract-type-
    specific shape (e.g., `invalid_chains` for ForbiddenContract); kept opaque
    here so the wrap doesn't need to know every contract type's schema."""

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    name: str
    contract_type: str
    kept: bool
    metadata: dict[str, object]
    warnings: tuple[str, ...]


class ContractsResult(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    kept: int
    broken: int
    module_count: int
    import_count: int
    contracts: tuple[ContractCheck, ...] = ()

    @property
    def all_kept(self) -> bool:
        return self.broken == 0


class ContractsNotAvailable(RuntimeError):
    """Raised when `import-linter` is not installed."""


class ContractsConfigError(RuntimeError):
    """Raised when the .importlinter file is missing or invalid."""


def run_contracts(
    project_dir: Path,
    config_filename: str | Path | None = None,
) -> ContractsResult:
    """Run import-linter against `project_dir` and return a structured result.

    `project_dir` must contain (or be the parent of) an importable copy of
    the package(s) named in the config; import-linter's graph builder uses
    runtime `import` resolution.

    Config resolution: `config_filename` (if given) wins; otherwise prefers
    `.importlinter` in `project_dir`; otherwise falls back to translating
    `archy.yaml` into Forbidden contracts. Raises `ContractsConfigError`
    if none are present.
    """
    try:
        from importlinter import configuration as _configuration  # noqa: F401
    except ImportError as exc:
        raise ContractsNotAvailable(
            "import-linter is not installed. "
            "Install with `pip install archy[contracts]` to use this feature."
        ) from exc
=== drive
def _drive_import_linter(
    *,
    config_path: Path | None = None,
    user_options: UserOptions | None = None,
) -> ContractsResult:
    """The narrow surface we depend on inside import-linter.

    Either pass `config_path` (we delegate reading to import-linter's
    INI/TOML readers) or pass pre-built `user_options` (used when we
    derive contracts from archy.yaml). Imports are deferred so the
    optional-dep guard in `run_contracts` triggers first.
    """
    from importlinter import configuration
    from importlinter.application.use_cases import (
        _register_contract_types,
        create_report,
        read_user_options,
    )

    configuration.configure()
    prior_cwd = Path.cwd()
    try:
        if user_options is None:
            assert config_path is not None
            # import-linter's INI reader resolves config_filename relative to
            # cwd; chdir into the config's directory for the duration of
            # read+report, then restore.
            os.chdir(config_path.parent)
            user_options = read_user_options(config_filename=config_path.name)
        _register_contract_types(user_options)
        report = create_report(user_options, cache_dir=None)
    finally:
        os.chdir(prior_cwd)

    contracts: list[ContractCheck] = []
    for contract, check in report.get_contracts_and_checks():
        contracts.append(
            ContractCheck(
                name=str(contract.name),
                contract_type=type(contract).__name__,
                kept=bool(check.kept),
                metadata=dict(check.metadata),
                warnings=tuple(check.warnings),
            )
        )
    return ContractsResult(
        kept=int(report.kept_count),
        broken=int(report.broken_count),
        module_count=int(report.module_count),
        import_count=int(report.import_count),
        contracts=tuple(contracts),
    )

def _expression_coverage(contract: object, graph: object) -> tuple[tuple[str, ...], bool]:
    """`(expressions matching no module, whether the contract could not fail)`.

    A contract whose `source_modules` (or any other populated module-expression
    field) resolves to nothing holds no matter what the code does, and
    import-linter reports it as kept. That is #435: the verdict is
    indistinguishable from a contract that was evaluated and held.

    Fields are read off the contract class's declared `*Field` descriptors, so
    every contract type that names modules is covered without this function
    knowing any of them. `LayersContract.layers` is the one gap: its module
    names sit inside `Layer` objects rather than in a flat expression
    collection, so a layers contract naming only absent modules is not flagged
    here. It is still caught for `containers`.
    """
    from importlinter.domain.helpers import module_expression_to_modules
    from importlinter.domain.imports import ModuleExpression

    unmatched: list[str] = []
    matched_nothing = False
    for name in _module_expression_fields(type(contract)):
        value = getattr(contract, name, None)
        expressions = [e for e in _as_iterable(value) if isinstance(e, ModuleExpression)]

            # claims nothing. Only a field the author DID fill in can lie.
            continue

        for expression in expressions:
            try:
                count = len(module_expression_to_modules(graph, expression))
            except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - a resolver error is not a verdict
                continue
            field_total += count
            if count == 0:
                unmatched.append(str(expression))
        if field_total == 0:
            matched_nothing = True
    return tuple(dict.fromkeys(unmatched)), matched_nothing


def _module_expression_fields(contract_type: type) -> tuple[str, ...]:

    Read from the class's `*Field` descriptors rather than a hardcoded list, so
    a new contract type in import-linter is covered the day it lands.

    from importlinter.domain.fields import ModuleExpressionField

    names: list[str] = []

        for name, field in vars(klass).items():
            subfield = getattr(field, "subfield", None)
            if isinstance(field, ModuleExpressionField) or isinstance(subfield, ModuleExpressionField):

def _to_import_linter_expressions(patterns: Iterable[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Translate archy layer patterns into import-linter module expressions.

    The two dialects disagree on one thing, and it is the one archy tells
    people to write. archy's `pkg.**` means "pkg AND every descendant"
    (`layers._translate_pattern` collapses the dot so the bare parent
    matches); import-linter's `pkg.**` means the descendants ONLY. So
    `shipping.store.**` on a leaf module resolved to the empty set, the
    Forbidden contract had no source modules, and a project with a real
    forbidden transitive path reported a clean pass at exit 0 (#435).

    Emitting the stem alongside the wildcard covers both halves of archy's
    meaning, and pairs with `as_packages: False` so descendants are not then
    folded in a second time by a different rule.
    """
    expressions: list[str] = []
    for pattern in patterns:

content.text: The walkthrough caught a real design error in my translation. With `as_packages: False`, a bare `shipping.api` pattern stops covering descendants, which changes behaviour well beyond #435. Reverting that half and keeping the translation minimal:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='src/archy/contracts.py'
s=open(p).read()

old = '''                # Each expression names exactly the modules archy's pattern
                # matches, so descendants must NOT be folded in a second time.
                "as_packages": "False",
'''
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, '', 1)

old_doc = '''    Emitting the stem alongside the wildcard covers both halves of archy's
    meaning, and pairs with `as_packages: False` so descendants are not then
    folded in a second time by a different rule.
    """
    expressions: list[str] = []
    for pattern in patterns:
        expressions.append(pattern)
        if pattern.endswith(".**"):
            expressions.append(pattern[: -len(".**")])
    return list(dict.fromkeys(expressions))'''
new_doc = '''    Dropping the trailing `.**` restores archy's meaning exactly, because
    import-linter's `as_packages` (on by default) already reads a named
    package as itself plus its descendants. Emitting the wildcard as well
    would add nothing and would report `pkg.**` as matching no module every
    time `pkg` is a leaf, which is noise archy itself generated.

    Nothing else is rewritten. A bare `pkg` keeps whatever `as_packages`
    gives it, which is how every existing config already behaves.
    """
    expressions: list[str] = []
    for pattern in patterns:
        expressions.append(pattern[: -len(".**")] if pattern.endswith(".**") else pattern)
    return list(dict.fromkeys(expressions))'''
assert old_doc in s
s = s.replace(old_doc, new_doc, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")
PYEOF

def test_run_contracts_clean_project_all_kept(
    tmp_path: Path, monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch
) -> None:
    _purge_top(monkeypatch)
    _write_fixture(tmp_path, with_violation=False)
    result = run_contracts(tmp_path)
    assert isinstance(result, ContractsResult)
    assert result.all_kept
    assert result.broken == 0
    assert result.kept == 1
    contract = result.contracts[0]
    assert contract.kept
    assert contract.contract_type == "ForbiddenContract"


def test_run_contracts_violation_surfaces_chain(
    tmp_path: Path, monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch
) -> None:
    _purge_top(monkeypatch)
    _write_fixture(tmp_path, with_violation=True)
    result = run_contracts(tmp_path)
    assert not result.all_kept
    assert result.broken == 1
    contract = result.contracts[0]
    assert not contract.kept
    chains = cast(list[dict[str, object]], contract.metadata.get("invalid_chains"))
    assert chains, "expected invalid_chains in violation metadata"
    chain = chains[0]
    # The shape import-linter exposes; surface it through the wrap unchanged.
    assert chain["downstream_module"] == "top.b"
    assert chain["upstream_module"] == "top.a"

def test_check_contracts_flag_nests_contract_results(tmp_path: Path):
    # #268: archy_check(contracts=True) folds the old archy_contracts tool,
    # nesting the transitive import-linter result under CheckPayload.contracts.
    # contracts=False (the default) leaves the field None, so a routine check
    # stays a pure direct-edge layer-rule result.
    pkg = tmp_path / "myapp"
    pkg.mkdir()
    (pkg / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    for sub in ("core", "cli"):
        (pkg / sub).mkdir()
        (pkg / sub / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (pkg / "core" / "api.py").write_text("")
    (pkg / "cli" / "runner.py").write_text("")
    _write_core_cli_forbid_config(tmp_path)

    server = create_server()
    path = str(tmp_path)

    # CheckPayload | CheckErrorPayload is a union return, so FastMCP wraps it
    # under a top-level `result` key (see the module docstring's wrapping rules).
    _c, plain = _call_tool(server, "archy_check", {"path": path})

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
fix(contracts): a forbidden transitive path no longer reports a clean pass

`archy contracts` reported `OK` at exit 0 on a project whose `store`
layer reaches `api` through `service`, which is exactly what a `forbid`
rule plus a transitive checker exists to catch (#435).

## Why

The two dialects disagree on the one form archy tells people to write.
archy's `pkg.**` means "pkg AND every descendant"; `layers.py`'s
translator collapses the dot so the bare parent matches. import-linter's
`pkg.**` means the descendants ONLY. So `shipping.store.**` on a leaf
module resolved to the empty set, the derived Forbidden contract had no
source modules, and import-linter kept it vacuously.

`check` had already told the user to come here: its output says "this
check governs too little of the graph to verify them; `archy check
--contracts` evaluates them transitively". Following that advice
produced more confidence and no more protection.

Dropping the trailing `.**` restores archy's meaning exactly, because
import-linter's `as_packages` (on by default) already reads a named
package as itself plus its descendants. Nothing else is rewritten: a
bare `pkg` keeps the behaviour every existing config already has, which
`bench/walkthrough.py` pins.

## A verdict that could not have failed is now said out loud

The ticket's general point, which outlives this particular translation

gh pr create --title "fix(contracts): a forbidden transitive path no longer reports a clean pass" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Closes #435.

## The bug

`archy contracts` reported `OK` at exit 0 on a project whose `store` layer reaches `api` through `service` — exactly what a `forbid` rule plus a transitive checker exists to catch.

The two dialects disagree on the one form archy tells people to write:

| pattern | archy's meaning | import-linter's meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pkg.**` | pkg **and** every descendant | the descendants **only** |

`layers.py`'s translator collapses the dot so the bare parent matches; import-linter's does not. So `shipping.store.**` on a leaf module resolved to the **empty set**, the derived Forbidden contract had no source modules, and import-linter kept it vacuously.

This was the recommended config, not an exotic one. `check` had already sent the user here:

```
#   1 forbid rule declared, but this check governs too little of the graph to verify them.
#   `archy check --contracts` evaluates them transitively via import-linter, which sees paths a direct-edge check cannot.
```

Following that advice produced more confidence and no more protection.

## The fix

Drop the trailing `.**` when deriving contracts, because import-linter's `as_packages` (on by default) already reads a named package as itself plus its descendants. That restores archy's meaning exactly.

Nothing else is rewritten. A bare `pkg` keeps the behaviour every existing config already has — an earlier draft of this patch also set `as_packages: False` for exact per-pattern fidelity, and `bench/walkthrough.py` caught that it silently changed how bare patterns behave. Reverted; that is a separate decision, not part of this fix.

## The general point, which outlives the translation bug

A contract that matched no module holds whatever the code does, and reporting it identically to one that was evaluated and held is what made the original defect invisible. Module expressions are now resolved against the graph:

```
# contracts: 1 kept, 0 broken (3 modules, 1 imports), 1 unverifiable
?? store layer must not reach api layer  [ForbiddenContract]
    ! could not have failed: no module matched, so this contract holds whatever the code does
    ! matched no module: top.*.handlers
```

Expressions are read off the contract class's declared `*Field` descriptors, so contract types this code has never heard of are covered. (`LayersContract.layers` is the documented gap: its module names sit inside `Layer` objects rather than a flat collection.)

`all_kept` keeps its meaning (nothing broken); a new `verified` says what callers actually want — evaluated **and** held. Both `verified` and `unverifiable` are `@computed_field`, since consumers read them off `model_dump()`, which drops a plain `@property` silently.

**Three surfaces**, wired in this change: CLI text (the `??` marker, the reason, the unmatched expressions, an `unverifiable` count), CLI JSON (`verified`, `unverifiable`, per-contract `matched_nothing` and `unmatched_expressions`), and the MCP `ContractsPayload`.

## A traceback the fix would otherwise have exposed

Once patterns resolve to real module names, a typo reaches import-linter's `_check_all_modules_exist_in_graph`, which aborts the whole run with a bare `ValueError: Module 'x' does not exist.` — a traceback that reads as archy being broken rather than the config. It is now a `ContractsConfigError` naming the config and how to list the modules archy discovered.

## Behaviour changes

- `archy contracts` exits 1 when a contract could not have failed. That is the point of the ticket: exit 0 on an unfalsifiable contract is the false pass. A config with a dead pattern will start failing, which is the population that was silently unprotected.
- `archy check --contracts` is unchanged in exit code (it reports; it has never gated), but its contracts payload now carries `verified`/`unverifiable`.

## Tests

Ten, each building a real package on disk and going through `run_contracts` or the command under test. All verified by mutation, `__pycache__` cleared between runs:

| mutation | tests that go red |
|---|---|
| pass patterns through unchanged (the bug) | 8, across all three surfaces |
| never set `matched_nothing` | 4 |
| exit on `all_kept` rather than `verified` | 1 |
| `verified` hardcoded `False` | 1 |
| drop the `ValueError` wrapper | 1 |

Scenarios: the ticket's own transitive path under `.**` patterns; the bare and `.**` dialects reaching the same verdict (they did not before, which is the bug); a wildcard matching no module; a named module absent from the graph; and the derived fields surviving `model_dump()`.

## Gates

`ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `ty check`, `pytest` (1,240 passed, up 9), `archy check`, `archy cycles --strict`, `archy conventions --emit-headers --check` all green.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_01THKU75bbbtU5yyUiXDDHbA
EOF

content.text:
**#435 fixed — PR #456:** https://github.com/hslee16/Archy/pull/456

The root cause turned out to be a dialect mismatch on the one pattern form archy tells people to write:

| pattern | archy | import-linter |
|---|---|---|
| `pkg.**` | pkg **and** descendants | descendants **only** |

So `shipping.store.**` resolved to the empty set, the derived contract had no source modules, and import-linter kept it vacuously. Since `check` explicitly hands users to `contracts` when its own coverage is thin, following that advice produced more confidence and no more protection.

Beyond the translation fix, I implemented the ticket's general point: a contract that matched no module is now reported as `??` with the reason, counted as `unverifiable`, and fails the exit code. `all_kept` keeps its meaning; a new `verified` says "evaluated **and** held." Both are `@computed_field` so they survive `model_dump()`.

**Three things the work surfaced that I didn't expect:**

1. **`bench/walkthrough.py` caught a design error of mine.** My first translation also set `as_packages: False` for exact per-pattern fidelity — which silently changed how bare `pkg` patterns behave, well beyond this bug. The walkthrough test failed and I reverted that half.
2. **The fix exposed a traceback.** Once patterns resolve to real module names, a typo hits import-linter's existence check and aborts the run with a bare `ValueError: Module 'x' does not exist.` Now a `ContractsConfigError` naming the config and how to list discovered modules.
3. **A behaviour change worth your attention:** `archy contracts` now exits 1 when a contract could not have failed. Configs with dead patterns will start failing — which is exactly the population that was silently unprotected, but it is a change existing users will notice.

Ten tests, all mutation-verified (8 die on reverting the translation, 4 on never flagging `matched_nothing`, and one each on three more mutants). 1,240 passing, all gates green.

Eleven review agents are running on it now — including the `cli_mcp_surface_parity` rule, which is the one that matters most here given the three surfaces.

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/issues -f title='check: `transitive_checked` is true even when every contract was unverifiable' -f body='Raised by the `cli_mcp_surface_parity` review round on PR #456 and split out, because resolving it is a wire-visible semantic decision on `check` and `brief`, not part of the #435 fix.

## What happens

#456 gives a contract result two new facts: `verified` (evaluated AND held) and `unverifiable` (how many contracts could not have failed because their module expressions matched nothing). `archy contracts` reads them, so it now exits 1 rather than reporting a clean pass.

`_transitive_checked` in `src/archy/cli.py` does not:

```python
def _transitive_checked(outcome: ContractsOutcome | None) -> bool:
    return outcome is not None and outcome.result is not None
```

It answers "did this run reach a verdict", and an unverifiable contract IS a verdict as far as that predicate is concerned. So `archy check --contracts --format json` can report `transitive_checked: true` with `transitive_unverified_reason: null` on a run where every `forbid` rule was evaluated against nothing. The same value flows to `brief` and to `archy_check(contracts=True)` on the MCP surface.

That is the #435 shape one surface further out: the run says the rules were checked transitively, and they were not.

## Why it needs a decision, not just a patch

Where the line sits is a real choice, and it changes a documented field:

1. **All-or-nothing.** `transitive_checked` is false only when there was at least one contract and every one was unverifiable. Conservative, but a run with one real contract and three dead ones still reads as fully checked.
2. **Any.** False as soon as any contract is unverifiable. Strictest, and the one that matches how `verified` behaves in #456, but it will flip the field for existing configs that have a dead pattern alongside live ones.
3. **Keep the predicate, extend the reason.** `transitive_checked` keeps meaning "reached a verdict", and `transitive_unverified_reason` (or a new field) carries the unverifiable count. Nothing existing flips; a reader has to consult two fields.

There is also the zero-contract case to settle: a config with no `forbid` rules at all currently reports `transitive_checked: true`, which options 1 and 2 leave alone but which has the same vacuity smell.

`README.md` and both copies of `skills/archy/SKILL.md` document `transitive_checked` explicitly, so whichever option wins has to reach them too.

## Related

- #435 and PR #456, which added `verified` / `unverifiable`
- #343, which is where `transitive_checked` came from: telling "checked transitively and clean" apart from "never looked"

content.text:
**#435 is fixed and PR #456 has been through a full review round.**

**Review results: 11 agents, 9 clean, 2 with findings — both fixed and now re-reviewed.**

1. **Doc-sync (the substantive one).** The agent-facing docs enumerated every other qualifier on a clean verdict — `coverage`, `transitive_checked`, `min_layers_present`, `required_violations` — and stopped short of the one this PR added. So README's `archy_check` row and both copies of SKILL.md still implied "did not fail" means "protected", which is precisely the reading #435 exists to kill. Fixed in all three files (the two SKILL.md copies are byte-identical by test).
2. **DRY in my new tests.** Two of the tests I added inlined the same two-module fixture instead of using the file's `_write_*_fixture` convention. Extracted. This was my code, not pre-existing, so I fixed rather than filed it.

Worth noting the doc-sync reviewer called `mark_review_as_passed` before finishing its analysis and then corrected itself, saying the review should have failed. Its findings were right, so I acted on them rather than on the recorded verdict.

**Filed, not folded in: #457.** The parity reviewer spotted that `_transitive_checked` in `cli.py` still answers "did this run reach a verdict", so `check --contracts --format json` can report `transitive_checked: true` with a null reason on a run where every `forbid` rule was evaluated against nothing. That's the #435 shape one surface further out — but fixing it means choosing between three semantics for a documented field that flows to `check`, `brief`, and the MCP surface, and it would flip the field for existing configs. That's your call, not mine to make inside this PR.

All gates green: 1,240 tests, ruff, ty, and archy's three self-checks.

PR #456 is ready to merge: https://github.com/hslee16/Archy/pull/456

content.content:
### Transitive contracts (`archy contracts`)

`archy check` only sees direct edges. `archy contracts` wraps [import-linter](https://import-linter.readthedocs.io/) so the same layer story is enforced *transitively* (A → B → C still counts as A reaching C). It is the strictness upgrade for projects whose layers leak through indirect paths.

```bash
pip install 'archy[contracts]'
archy contracts path/to/project
archy contracts path/to/project --format json
```

`archy check --contracts` runs this same transitive verdict inline, nested under the check output. It never changes `check`'s own exit code: a flag that can turn a passing check into a failing one because an optional dependency is absent would be unsafe to leave on in CI. Use the standalone `archy contracts` when the transitive result should itself gate the build.

**Config resolution.** `archy contracts` reads, in order:

1. The `--config` argument if passed.
2. `.importlinter` in the project root: the **canonical** contracts config.
3. `archy.yaml`: best-effort fallback. Each `forbid:` rule becomes one Forbidden contract checked transitively. Emits a `UserWarning` because this path cannot express `ignore_imports`, so any legitimate transitive edge (e.g., a service layer reaching `psycopg` *through* a sanctioned `app.libs.db.*` module) will be reported as a violation with no way to whitelist it.

Two configs, one concern each:

- **`archy.yaml`** owns layer definitions, direct-edge gating (`archy check`), required-reach rules (`required:`), `sdp:`, `exclude:`, and `roots:`.
- **`.importlinter`** owns transitive contracts: all five contract types (Forbidden, Layers, Independence, Protected, AcyclicSiblings) and `ignore_imports` whitelists.

Reach for `.importlinter` as soon as you need transitive enforcement at all; the archy.yaml fallback is a zero-config onramp, not a feature target. See [`.importlinter`](.importlinter) in this repo for a real-world example, and the [import-linter contract types reference](https://import-linter.readthedocs.io/en/stable/contract_types.html) for the full grammar.

Common case: forbid services from reaching `psycopg` but allow the sanctioned db library to do so:

```ini
[importlinter]
root_package = app

[importlinter:contract:services-must-not-reach-psycopg]
name = services must not reach psycopg

content.text: Correct — my README sentence was an unqualified claim while the detector has a documented gap for `layers` contracts. Fixing the claim and filing the gap:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='README.md'
s=open(p).read()
old = "`--format json` adds top-level `verified` and `unverifiable` alongside `kept`/`broken`, and per-contract `matched_nothing` and `unmatched_expressions`.\n"
new = ("`--format json` adds top-level `verified` and `unverifiable` alongside `kept`/`broken`, and per-contract "
       "`matched_nothing` and `unmatched_expressions`. One gap, for `.importlinter` configs: a `type = layers` "
       "contract keeps its module names inside `Layer` objects rather than a flat expression field, so layer names "
       "that match nothing are not flagged (its `containers` are). The `archy.yaml` fallback derives only Forbidden "
       "contracts, which are covered.\n")
assert old in s
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(old, new, 1))
print("ok")
PYEOF
gh api repos/:owner/:repo/issues -f title='contracts: a `layers` contract naming only absent modules is still not flagged as unverifiable' -f body='Split out of PR #456 (which closes #435), where the gap is documented rather than closed.

## The gap

#456 resolves each contract'"'"'s module expressions against the graph and flags a contract that could not have failed. `_expression_coverage` finds the expressions by reading the contract class'"'"'s declared `*Field` descriptors, which covers every contract type whose module names sit in a flat `SetField`/`ListField` of `ModuleExpressionField`:

- `ForbiddenContract.source_modules` / `.forbidden_modules` — covered
